title: High School Science Profile Predicts Adults’ Views on the Future of AI and STS
extended_summary:
This paper asks whether high school science experiences are associated with how adults later use artificial intelligence (AI) and how they think about the social implications of AI and science-technology-society (STS) issues. The motivation is the growing importance of preparing students for an AI-shaped future, alongside a lack of longitudinal evidence linking K-12 science education to adult AI engagement.

The study uses longitudinal data from the Korea Employment Education Panel (KEEP) II, following a cohort of Korean general high school students from 2016 to 2023. The sample includes 2,348 individuals. The analysis is not an intervention study; instead, it examines associations among high school science interest and achievement, adult AI use, perceived positive and negative consequences of AI, and STS views using structural equation modeling.

Results suggest that high school science achievement predicted later AI use, whereas science interest did not directly predict AI use. AI use was associated with both positive and negative perceptions of AI, and these perceptions in turn related to more nuanced views about human-AI relations, future quality of life, and monopolization of science and technology benefits. The study concludes that secondary science education may have long-term relevance for adults’ engagement with AI and their broader technology-related beliefs, though the evidence is correlational rather than causal.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed longitudinal correlational study using panel data and SEM, which provides useful observational evidence but no experimental control or causal identification. It is methodologically stronger than a cross-sectional survey, but still has key credibility limits for attributing effects.
impact_tier_rationale: The observed downstream association from science achievement to AI use is modest (β=.18) and pertains to adults rather than a direct K-12 learning intervention. It suggests potentially meaningful long-run institutional relevance, but the paper does not test an educational technology or show immediate instructional impact.

finding.finding_summary: In a longitudinal panel study of n=2,348 South Korean general high school students followed from 2016/2017 to 2023, high school science achievement significantly predicted later AI use in adulthood (β=.18, p<.001), but science interest did not (β=-.007, n.s.). AI use then predicted adults’ AI perceptions and STS views, suggesting K-12 science profiles have downstream effects on technology-related beliefs rather than direct immediate academic outcomes.
finding.measure: Structural equation modeling of self-reported AI use, AI positive/negative perceptions, and STS views in adulthood, predicted from high school science interest and achievement
